query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal‐element alloys used at high temperatures, the oxidation resistance and long‐term integrity are governed by the rapid formation of a thin, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale enriched in key elements (e.g., Al or Cr) that preferentially diffuse to the surface. This protective scale limits further oxidation and stabilizes the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal‐element alloy with a well‐mixed single-phase or dual-phase microstructure, having a baseline composition with moderate levels of elements like Al or Cr.
generation.intervention: Increase the concentration of protective alloying elements (e.g., Al, Cr) or design a variant with locally enriched regions to promote enhanced surface oxidation behavior.
generation.conditions: Expose test samples to high-temperature oxidizing environments (800–1200 °C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures for extended periods.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent and continuous oxide layer at the alloy surface, where the scale’s adhesion and uniformity are mediated by the selective segregation and oxidation of Al/Cr at the grain boundaries and surface regions.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, diffusion of key protective elements (e.g., Al or Cr) to the surface leads to the rapid development of a coherent, slow-growing oxide (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3). This scale serves as a physical barrier, reducing the rate of further oxygen ingress and metal loss, and maintains the bulk material’s structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The variant with higher levels of protective elements will form a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scale; it will exhibit lower weight gains and reduced scale spallation compared to the baseline alloy, thereby showing improved oxidation resistance and better preservation of mechanical integrity over time.
generation.baseline: The multiprincipal‐element alloy with the original composition (i.e., moderate protective element levels) that is expected to develop a less continuous and more rapidly growing oxide scale under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold over the temperature range of 800 °C to 1200 °C in environments with controlled oxygen partial pressures. Deviations may occur at temperatures below 800 °C (where oxidation kinetics are slower) or above 1200 °C (where scale breakdown or volatilization of oxides might change the mechanism).
generation.uncertainty: The precise effect size (e.g., reduction in oxide thickness or weight gain) is uncertain without quantitative studies, and the interplay of other minor alloying elements and microstructural features may modulate the observed behavior. Scale adhesion mechanisms might also vary with processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multiprincipal‐element alloy samples: one with the baseline composition and another modified to have an increased concentration of protective elements (e.g., Al, Cr). Expose both sets to identical high-temperature (800–1200 °C) oxidizing conditions for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface oxide layer (using SEM/EDS, XRD, TEM) and measure weight gain over time.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity via cross-sectional microscopy
Phase identification of the oxide formed (e.g., presence of Al2O3 or Cr2O3) via XRD
Mechanical adhesion of the scale (e.g., via scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy variant with higher protective element concentrations does not demonstrate a significantly thinner, more adherent, and more stable oxide scale (i.e., shows similar or inferior oxidation behavior, weight gain, and spallation) relative to the baseline alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that enhanced selective oxidation of Al/Cr governs improved high-temperature oxidation resistance would be falsified.
